_meta.note: Per-mission historical commentary takes for Kestrel Heavy (DECISIONS #77, PR #449). Source of truth for generation; docs/plans/per-mission-commentary.md renders the same lines in readable tables. Each take is one single-speaker color-layer line (layer=color, interruptible=true), gated by requires.mission so it only ever plays on its own mission. Real names appear ONLY in these lines. No invented quotes; the single verbatim quote (m17-coa-1, Armstrong) is flagged in the plan doc.
_meta.rules: Every line at most 14 words (WRITING_BIBLE 6.2 / color lint). No line states a fact about the flown design (no engine counts, no 'booster', no strap-ons, no Haven/pad/site claims) so the claim-vs-design verifier stays green with claims ['mission'] only.

takes.text: In 1926, Robert Goddard flew the first liquid-fuel rocket.
It rose forty-one feet, in two and a half seconds.
Goddard launched from a farm field in Massachusetts.
It burned gasoline and liquid oxygen, not gunpowder.
One hundred kilometres up is the edge of space.
The line is a convention, set in 1960 for record keeping.
Above the line, the air is too thin for wings.
The first American in space flew above this line in 1961.
On October 4, 1957, Sputnik became the first satellite.
It weighed about eighty-four kilograms, a beach ball with antennas.
Sputnik circled Earth once every ninety-six minutes.
Its beep was heard by radio operators around the world.
On April 1, 1960, TIROS-1 became the first weather satellite.
It carried two television cameras and weighed two hundred seventy pounds.
TIROS-1 sent back nineteen thousand usable pictures in seventy-eight days.
Forecasters saw cloud patterns from space for the first time.
The Saturn V stood one hundred eleven metres tall.
Five F-1s made seven and a half million pounds of thrust.
It could lift one hundred forty tonnes to low Earth orbit.
Thirteen Saturn Vs flew, and none ever lost crew or payload.
On December 21, 2015, a Falcon 9 first stage landed upright.
It touched down at Landing Zone 1, nine minutes after liftoff.
Before that, no orbital first stage had ever landed.
In 2024, Starship's first stage was caught by its tower.
In December 2015, a Falcon 9 booster became the first from an orbital launch to land upright.
Landing ships wait far downrange, so the booster needn't fly all the way back.
A transfer orbit stretches from low orbit out to thirty-six thousand kilometres.
The first droneship landing was a Falcon 9, in April 2016.
On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
His flight lasted one hundred eight minutes, launch to landing.
One orbit proved a person could live and work in space.
In 1962, John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth.
In September 1959, Luna 2 became the first object to reach the Moon.
It flew thirty-six hours and struck the Moon at three kilometres per second.
Luna 2 carried no engine of its own, only instruments and pennants.
In 1968, Apollo 8 carried the first crew around the Moon.
Falcon Heavy is three Falcon 9 first stages strapped side by side.
Twenty-seven Merlins lit together on its first flight in 2018.
Its first payload was a red Tesla Roadster, with a mannequin driver.
The two side boosters landed together, eight minutes after liftoff.
Landsat 1 launched July 23, 1972, to map Earth's resources.
It flew a sun-synchronous orbit, crossing the equator at the same morning hour.
Its orbit repeated every eighteen days, imaging the whole planet.
Landsat began the longest Earth-observation program ever flown.
Hubble launched aboard Space Shuttle Discovery in April 1990.
It orbits about five hundred forty kilometres up, above the blurring air.
Its mirror was flawed, and astronauts fixed it in orbit in 1993.
Five shuttle crews serviced Hubble, the last in 2009.
The CubeSat standard was drawn up in 1999, a ten-centimetre cube.
The first CubeSats flew in June 2003, built mostly by students.
One Falcon 9 flight carried one hundred forty-three satellites at once.
That rideshare beat the old record of one hundred four satellites.
In October 2012, Dragon flew the first commercial cargo run to the station.
It carried about nine hundred kilograms of supplies to the station.
The station's robotic arm caught Dragon and berthed it.
Dragon could bring cargo back down, not just carry it up.
In 1964, Syncom 3 became the first satellite to hold still over Earth.
It relayed the Tokyo Olympics live from Japan to America.
Early Bird followed in 1965, the first commercial satellite of its kind.
Early Bird carried two hundred forty phone calls at once.
People have lived aboard the space station without a break since 2000.
Expedition 1 arrived on November 2, three people in three modules.
Crews hand the station over in person, so the chain never breaks.
The station hosts crews from five space agencies working together.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, atop a Saturn V.
Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20.
Armstrong flew the lander by hand past a rocky crater.
That is one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.
takes.verbatimQuote: Armstrong, July 20 1969 (NASA transcript); the only verbatim quote in this set.

takes.text: New Horizons left Earth faster than any spacecraft before it.
It passed the Moon's orbit in just nine hours.
Nine years later it flew past Pluto, twelve thousand five hundred kilometres away.
It kept flying, past Arrokoth, the most distant world ever visited.
March 2017, a Falcon 9 flew again, the first reused orbital rocket.
That stage had already flown a station cargo run in 2016.
It landed again on a droneship, the first stage to fly twice.
Today, single first stages have flown more than thirty times each.
Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and is still flying, past the planets.
It crossed into interstellar space in 2012, the first spacecraft to do so.
Its golden record carries greetings in fifty-five languages.
Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object from Earth.
